posts.c: Vermont’s regular deer season kicked off on Saturday, and for the first time in almost 40 years, hunters can now obtain a permit to shoot a deer without antlers — including does — with a rifle. Previously, most hunters were only allowed to harvest antlerless deer during archery season and muzzleloader season, which requires a different kind of gun and is far less popular than rifle hunting. Novice and youth hunters were allowed to shoot antlerless deer. Now, hunters can obtain an antlerless deer permit for a specific area of the state and use it during the rifle season. Biologists with the state say the change is needed to control Vermont’s deer population. But at the West Enosburg Country Store, a popular weigh station in Franklin County, hunters were divided over whether the change is a good thing. Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photos courtesy of Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife and Abagael Giles/Vermont Public.
posts.hd: Vermont hunters divided over new deer regulations

posts.c: Stressing that this was the last thing he needed after three months of chemotherapy, local cancer patient Robert Marcinik was reportedly shocked to learn Thursday that he had been charged an extra $2,000 to ring the bell. “I rang the bell to mark the end of my lung cancer treatment, and now I have this surprise bill from my insurance company because apparently it’s not covered,” said Marcinik, adding that the weakness and nausea he had experienced from weeks of chemo paled in comparison to the stomach-churning realization that clanging the bell was considered an adjuvant therapy requiring pre-authorization. “The bell at the hospital is out-of-network, and according to Blue Cross Blue Shield, I should have used the in-network bell 40 miles from here. They said my oncologist should have written a referral to ring the bell, but even if he had, my HMO wouldn’t have covered it. Plus, each pull of the rope is an individual charge—I wish I hadn’t gone hog wild dinging that thing.” At press ti

The nominations for the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced Monday, and women across genres dominated the major categories. This year’s nominees for best new artist ranged from country to rap to indie rock.⁠ ⁠ On the alternative side, there’s the Brooklyn rock band Geese and the mask-wearing math rock duo, Angine de Poitrine. Country singer Ella Langley, electropop star Slayyyter and the quirky pop-funk of Remi Wolf also got nods. So did the rapper Don Toliver. And for fans of a throwback soul and R&B sound, there’s English singer Sienna Spiro. And also the Womack Sisters, a girl group formed by the granddaughters of Sam Cooke.⁠ ⁠ All eight acts will compete for best new artist at the Grammys ceremony in February.⁠ ⁠ Find “NPR News Now” wherever you listen to podcasts.⁠ ⁠ And tap the link in our bio to read the full story.⁠ (Link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-6037518/2027-grammy-nominations-complete-list)⁠ ⁠ Host: Korva Coleman/NPR⁠ Reporter: Isabella Gomez Sarmiento/NPR⁠

posts.c: Observing that the search for nirvana was futile, onlookers confirmed Tuesday that the pack of teens moving between subway cars must not realize that enlightenment lies wherever they are. “These kids can spend the whole train ride moving from car to car, but they’ll be no closer to finding the inner peace they seek,” said fellow passenger Angela Azar, noting that the boisterous group of high schoolers reminded her of restless ghosts who bother the living because they are trapped, unable to move on to a higher realm. “Don’t these teens know that this car and each subsequent car they enter offers no more answers than the one where they began this journey? If they simply sat down on the first seat they saw, they could finally realize that the answers to the all the questions of the universe are within us. When they reach the end of the train, they’ll understand that their wandering was in vain and that they’ve wasted the entire trip seeking what wasn’t there.” Nearby passengers later adde

posts.c: In case you missed it, we put out an update on the 2026 ozone hole! Here’s what you missed: Earth’s protective ozone layer is still on track for long-term recovery, despite a larger Antarctic ozone hole this year because of a strong polar vortex. The 2026 ozone hole is the 7th-largest ozone hole since NASA began tracking it in 1979. This year, the ozone hole reached its maximum extent of 10.5 million square miles on September 18. Video description: Animation of stratospheric ozone concentration on a globe centered over Antarctica. Higher ozone concentrations are shown in reds, yellows, and greens. Lower ozone concentrations are shown in blues and purples. The animation starts in July 2026. A blue circle indicating the ozone hole begins to form in mid-August. It becomes larger and a darker shade of blue until the ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, 2026. The animation ends on October 5. Credit: NASA

posts.c: Vermont relies on a dozen or so local backcountry rescue teams, most staffed by volunteers. The Vermont State Police coordinate searches and call on those teams when people become stranded or go missing. Last year, state police recorded 120 search-and-rescue notifications or activations, the most since 2021 and well above the average of roughly 100 rescues annually during the previous decade. Fewer of those come from lost hikers, thanks to improved cellphone coverage and digital mapping apps, according to Lt. Thomas Howard. But growing interest in backcountry skiing and a better notification system between ski resorts and the state have contributed to an increase in skiing-related calls. Drew Clymer, the Department of Public Safety’s civilian search-and-rescue coordinator and deputy chief of Stowe Mountain Rescue, believes social media is increasingly leading unprepared people to venture into unsafe conditions. He recalled a man who became lost in the backcountry last year as a result

posts.c: 🦌...November is when most Vermont outdoorsfolk are thinking about deer, but for our fish culture staff November is also the month of salmon...🐟! Before European colonization, this time of year is when landlocked Atlantic salmon would swim into the tributaries of Vermont’s large lakes to spawn. Now, as we work to keep populations of these prized fish healthy and ultimately to restore them in their native waters, November is the time when we gather salmon eggs to rear in our hatcheries around the state. Pictured here, staff at our Bald Hill Fish Culture Station collect salmon eggs from hatchery-dwelling broodstock to supplement the eggs harvested from feral fish in Vermont's bigger waters of Lake Champlain, Lake Memphremagog, Lake Willoughby and Seymour Lake.

posts.c: “Every year when the calendar reaches the ninth month of the lunar calendar, Bangkok (and Thailand) enters the Vegetarian Festival,” says CNT Local Creator @ms_plengpanich. “Locally known as the Jay Festival, the nine-day Vegetarian Festival is how Thai-Chinese people observe tradition and reset their bodies. During this time, those who participate abstain from meat and certain other foods, and dress in white as a way of cleansing. Bangkok’s Chinatown streets come alive with yellow flags and vegetarian stalls. Toob tab, toob tab. The rhythmic sound draws a crowd to Toobtab Lao Pae, a third-generation sweet maker tucked in the alley beside Chou Zhou Kong Shrine in Talat Noi. This Thai-Chinese confection is deceptively simple to make. Peanuts and sugar are folded together and pounded by hand with a wooden hammer until the caramelized mixture turns crunchy. Its name is inspired by the distinct sound of the hammer, a sound that has become part of the neighborhood’s annual ritual. First est

posts.c: Last month, Welsh adventurer @ash_dykes set out on a nearly 500-mile kayaking expedition through the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest rainforest, alongside local guide @obedtemba and cameraman @willperezstory. Their journey quickly captivated millions online, offering an up-close look at a region unfamiliar to many. From spending the day with the Ba’Aka tribe to spotting forest elephants and outrunning swarms of bees, the team’s frequent social media videos kept viewers hooked—and even sparked concern when the crew suddenly went radio silent. But as the adventure went viral, it also opened the door to a much bigger conversation about how the Congo and its communities are portrayed to the outside world—and who gets to tell their stories. Read the full story at the link in bio. Images by: @obedtemba and @willperezstory
posts.hd: Kayaker's 500-mile Congo River expedition goes viral

posts.c: Why is it called Arches? Because “A lot of rocks with holes in them” didn’t test well. Well, not quite. Arches National Park, located in eastern Utah near the town of Moab, is world-famous for its extraordinary concentration of natural red-rock geology and dramatic desert landscapes. In fact, the park protects more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches, ranging from tiny openings to massive spans carved by wind, water, and underground salt movement. This red-rock wonderland will amaze you with its formations, refresh you with its trails, and inspire you with the views. NPS photos: @archesnps

posts.c: The Best Places to Go in 2027: The Albanian Alps "This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask," says writer @nomapsamber. "Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration." At the link in bio, read @nomapsamber’s full story on her journey through the Peaks of the Balkans, a trail that winds through some of the region’s most extraordinary landscapes. Images: @nomapsamber

posts.c: Punk rock icon Henry Rollins (@fanatichenry) moved to Nashville, the country music capital of the world, five years ago. He had built up a collection of punk posters, photographs and ephemera. Recently he produced a free show of his collection. This exhibition title? Cool Evidence. The 65-year old Rollins wanted to do a punk museum in Nashville. But after crunching the numbers he decided on a series of traveling pop-ups around the world. Music and Culture reporter Justin Barney (@justinbarney) attended the show. There were lines to get in that snaked around the gallery. The walls were chock full of colorful band posters. And they each had a written description from Rollins himself. And in the middle of the gallery, the biggest crowd was around Rollins himself, who held court all night, explaining his ethos for doing this. “Now that I’m old, my job is to find ways to release joy. I owe history to get this stuff out in front of people.” And in 2028, he hopes to take the exhibition on tou

posts.c: Over the past year, seven people were killed in crashes while biking, walking, and rolling on Vermont roadways: Mauricio Martinez, Janet Spencer, Kylee Bean, Owen Rich, Devin Pierro, Shiloh Skalka, and Todd Ward. On this World Day of Remembrance, we honor them, as well as the 139 more injured, and the impact left on their families, friends, and communities. It doesn’t have to be this way. What can you do? Know where to go in a time of crisis. Connect with advocates in your community, and stay connected with your walking/biking/rolling community - especially in the coming winter months. Find all of these resources, and our full report on the World Day of Remembrance at the link in our bio. #WDoR2026 #SafetyNotSpeed

posts.c: From the traditional music of Colombia's Pacific coast to Tego Calderón and Nigerian Afrobeats star Burna Boy, Colombian artist @jossmansaac takes us on a musical journey across the African diaspora. Recorded live in Bogotá during @bogotamusicmarket 2026, this episode of El Sonido: Cancioneros explores the connections between Timbiquí, the Caribbean, and Nigeria through the music that shaped Jossman's identity as a singer, songwriter, and producer. Known as AFROKING, Jossman has spent years building bridges between contemporary Afrobeats and the musical traditions of Colombia's Pacific coast. His 2025 album AFROKING brings those worlds together through collaborations with artists including Nidia Góngora and Grupo Canalón de Timbiquí. 📺 Watch the full video episode on the KEXP Podcasts YouTube channel or listen wherever you get your podcasts. Support El Sonido at kexp.org/el-sonido.

posts.c: My neighbor practically gave me this board so I'm doing my best to use it. It comes from an era where everything was made with big transformer preamps, and so models like this took on the colloquial name of "japa-neve", referencing the Rupert Neve design preamps (1073 and the like). Seeing as I've been on the dl looking for a 1073 style preamp, it could be a match made in heaven or it could be a total bust! I'm not about to debate that preamps are worthwhile to invest in. They almost certainly are not for the large majority of songwriters or home producers as most listeners, including audiophiles, probably couldn't tell the difference between a track that was produced with a thousand dollar preamp or your average focusrite 2i2. That said, I am (unfortunately) now able to hear the difference and so I want to have the option to use them if I can.

posts.c: In Vermont, the sugarhouse is a kind of sacred place: a steamy little cabin at the edge of the woods where sap becomes syrup and neighbors gather while the fire burns. It is fitting, then, that the state’s most talked-about new hotel takes its name and its spirit from them. @sugarhousehotelvt has opened in Winooski, a historic mill city just across the river from Burlington, and it is the first hotel the city has ever had. It is also something Marriott has never done anywhere in the world: a hotel designed from the start to run entirely on electricity, produce as much energy as it uses over the course of a year and earn LEED Platinum certification. And yet the first thing you notice isn’t the technology. It’s the timber, the glass and the sense that every corner was made by someone who lives nearby. → Read the full story on 5 Reasons to Visit. #travel #destination #vermont #winooski #newengland

posts.c: 💕 Did you know that WHERE you pet your dog matters? Our furry friends have their own preferences when it comes to physical touch! Some enjoy gentle chest rubs, chin scratches, and soft pets around the base of the neck. 🐾 Usually loved: Gentle chest rubs, chin scratches, and soft strokes along the back. ⚠️ Be careful with: Reaching over the head, touching the paws, hugging tightly, or pulling the tail. These actions can make some dogs feel uncomfortable or trapped. 💙 Every dog is different, so watch their body language and let them choose when they want affection. 👇 Question: Where does your dog love being petted the most?

posts.c: Every dad has given this exact look at least once 😂 Music production has become much more accessible in recent years, with software called a DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) allowing anyone with a laptop to create, record, and mix their own beats and tracks from home. What once required an expensive professional studio can now be done on a bedroom desk, which is why so many young people have picked it up as a hobby or even a career path. For parents, it can be hard to tell whether all those hours staring at a screen and tweaking sounds is serious creative work or just a very convincing way to avoid the dishes. (🎥/ @v.v.j._trey )

posts.c: The flies didn’t stand a chance 😂 Salt guns are handheld devices designed to shoot a small burst of regular table salt at insects, killing or stunning them on contact. They are popular because the salt disperses quickly and leaves no toxic residue, making them safer to use around food than chemical sprays. The range and spread of the salt means they work best at close distances, and while they are effective against flies and similar insects, they do leave a light dusting of salt on whatever surface is nearby, which can be a small downside at the dinner table. (🎥/ @lindybowbindy )

posts.c: Presented by National Geographic Society in partnership with @Rolex. Pygmy blue whales compete with fin whales for the title of the second-largest animal in the world. They typically roam the world’s oceans, but one group off the coast of New Zealand seems to have settled in the South Taranaki Bight. To better understand the behavior of these marine giants, researchers are studying some of the ocean’s smallest creatures—swarms of krill thriving in the whales’ new home. They hope that by understanding the relationship between the two, they can better understand the effects that warming waters will have on them. Learn more about this mysterious group of whales at the link in bio. Rolex and the National Geographic Society are partnering on select science-based expeditions to explore, study, and document change in the planet’s unique regions. #PerpetualPlanet. Videos by National Geographic Society/Impact Story Lab; Photographs by @ralphpace

posts.c: “I don’t think about the listener. I just make it because I want to make it.” As part of EMERGENT with Levi’s®, Yuki Chiba (@yukichiba_) talks about making music without overthinking it, from improvising in the studio to songwriting as a way of documenting life as it happens. Set reminder for the premiere via the link in bio.

9 years ago, we made a song called Santorini. At the time, it became our most successful release, finding its way around the world and reaching over 2 million streams. We never could have imagined that almost a decade later we’d find ourselves standing in the very place that inspired its name. It felt surreal making music together in the studio to watching the sun set over the Aegean Sea, surrounded by blue domes, and walking through the whitewashed streets. A pretty special full circle moment. Forever grateful for the music, the memories, and the journey. 💙🇬🇷

posts.c: Lord Voldemort’s name contains a hidden secret that reveals his true identity! In the Harry Potter series, “Tom Marvolo Riddle” is an anagram of “I am Lord Voldemort,” a clever detail created by author J.K. Rowling. Even more surprisingly, Voldemort was born on December 31, 1926, making him 71 years old when he died during the Battle of Hogwarts in 1998. Despite his obsession with immortality, he died younger than many ordinary wizards. Voldemort’s terrifying appearance wasn’t how he originally looked. As a young man, Tom Riddle was described as exceptionally handsome, but his experiments with dark magic gradually transformed his appearance. He created multiple Horcruxes by splitting his soul, believing they would protect him from death. Ironically, his desperate attempts to become immortal ultimately contributed to his destruction, making one of fiction’s most feared villains a character whose greatest weakness was his fear of dying. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes

posts.c: Photo by @joelsartore | This brightly colored serpent is an ornate palm pit viper that I photographed @sanantoniozoo. In the wild, the species can be found in the cloud forests of Mexico and northern Guatemala. Unfortunately, this snake’s habitat is used frequently for agricultural purposes—growing coffee plants and ornamental ferns—which has decreased suitable habitat. You can do your part to protect the snake by purchasing wildlife-friendly coffee and growing plants native to your region in your outdoor spaces. To see more species featured in the Photo Ark, follow me, @joelsartore. #PhotoArk

posts.c: Believe it or not, these magical berries are real! ✨ This is wild grape, also known as porcelain berry (Ampelopsis glandulosa var. brevipedunculata) It’s a close relative of the true grape (Vitus), and the two can be difficult to tell apart when they aren’t in fruit. The easiest way to tell the difference is to break a stem. While the wild grape has a white pith, the true grape has a brown pith 🍇 ⚠️ A reminder that these berries aren't for eating and while very beautiful, the plant is considered invasive in some areas. 📍Agius Evolution Garden

posts.c: Take a look at this melanistic leopard 🖤 "This photograph is one of my favorites of a very special creature, a female melanistic leopard named Giza, born in 2021 in the wilderness of Laikipia. If somebody had told me twenty years before that exactly on the day of my fiftieth birthday, August 19th 2025, I would be photographing a black leopard with a 50mm lens, I would have thought they were completely crazy! Until 2022, the mere possibility of even spotting a black leopard in Kenya was beyond anyone’s dream. But something incredible occurred in this rugged and wild region of Kenya. The melanistic gene began spreading successfully through the population of leopards, causing an increase in the incidence of this rare mutation. In a savannah habitat, black leopards would normally be disadvantaged, as they would be easy target for lions, and would be too visible to their prey. posts.c: Kim Jong Un reportedly brought his own toilet when traveling abroad! According to South Korean intelligence reports, the North Korean leader uses a private toilet to prevent foreign intelligence agencies from collecting biological samples that could reveal information about his health. His security arrangements are so elaborate that bodyguards have been filmed jogging alongside his moving limousine. Even more surprisingly, Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood attending school in Switzerland under an assumed identity, where former classmates described him as a basketball enthusiast who admired Michael Jordan. Despite ruling one of the world’s most isolated countries, he has met former NBA star Dennis Rodman multiple times, and the two developed an unlikely friendship that attracted worldwide attention. posts.c: Next Tuesday, November 24th, we're gathering downstairs for our monthly Helping Hands: Quilts for the Community event, and we would love for you to join us for the last sew-in of 2026. From 1 to 4pm, customers and staff come together to finish quilts that are donated to local organizations, including Laurie's House, Steps to End Domestic Violence, the Lund Home, the Respite House, and the Refugee Resettlement Center. All skill levels are welcome, and there are plenty of jobs that don't require a sewing machine. We provide tables, chairs, cutting mats, irons, and ironing boards. posts.c: Spot the difference 👁️ Alex Visbal (@alexvisbal) is working on a long-term project documenting the industrial footprint on bodies of water, and this photo shows how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. The distinctive pink colour on the left is caused by bright pink microbes that thrive in extremely saline water, which happens when an area is cut off from a supply of fresh water. The ecology of the lake is in sharp decline due to industrial use, upstream diversions and climate change. Since this image was taken, the State of Utah has brought the area under conservation management. 📸 ‘The Great Divide’ is the winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year. Book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio! #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #USA #Utah

posts.c: A caracal mother and cub 🧡 "When I moved to my tent just outside the Maasai Mara NR in 2007 and I became a full-time photographer, one particular creature was considered a sort of holy-grail for wildlife photographers working in Africa. It was rarely if ever seen, and the few sightings were just fleeting glimpses shooting across a track, or shadows in the dark night. One morning I was driving in the central Mara when I spotted a small predator jumping on a termite mound in the distance, immediately followed by a second one. I grabbed my binoculars and realised I was looking at two caracals. As they disappeared back in the long grass, I drove closer and after a long search, found them again, almost invisible, crouched in a small clump of grass. That moment marked the beginning of one of my most unforgettable stories in the wild. I followed this mother caracal and her curious male cub for a few months, until the evening when this photograph was taken, the last one they spent together bef

posts.c: “Touch grass” is an ancient internet expression used to remind people that there is an outside. An area beyond the computer or phone screen where plants grow and people occasionally make eye contact. Not too much eye contact. Let’s not be weird. The phrase is believed to have originated among online users who noticed that other online users were becoming increasingly unpleasant. Rather than explain this to them, they suggested they go outside and touch a plant. What did the plant ever do? Scientists have yet to establish whether touching grass actually improves someone’s mood or feelings. Early research suggests it does stop people from posting online anywhere between never and three seconds. It’s a start. The National Park Service has been encouraging people to get outdoors since 1916. So this weekend, consider logging off and getting outdoors. Your outlook on things might just improve. Have a great weekend. Tell us about it on Monday. NPS Photos

posts.c: The highly limited, large-scale collector’s edition of Reverence is officially available for purchase. Truthfully, when I asked for this edition to be made, I expected the answer to be “Impossible.” I am utterly obsessed with the idea of seeing my images printed as big as I can imagine. If I could see one of my icebergs or elephants the size of a building, looming larger than life, I would be over the moon. The challenge with printing images at such a scale is that quality tends to diminish as the pixels are stretched beyond their capacity. But the expert printers behind this very special edition of Reverence worked what can only be described as magic, bringing every detail into sharper focus than even my own memory. posts.c: With the monitoring season for our Champlain Aquatic invasive Monitoring Program (CHAMP) coming to a close, let's take a look back on what we found! 47 sites and 122 surveys later, zebra mussels and Eurasian watermilfoil were tied for the most frequently reported species (both reported in 61% of surveys). Water chestnut was reported in 11% of surveys, and brittle naiad in 6% of surveys. A CHAMP volunteer reported the first golden clam in Lake Champlain during a survey in Whitehall, NY in 2024, and it was found there again in 2025. Despite regular surveying at the original detection site, golden clam was not reported through CHAMP in 2026. New York and Vermont state partners have also surveyed nearby areas, and as of now, golden clam has not been detected outside the original CHAMP site. Some good news on top of that: zero species on the CHAMP "watchlist" (species not yet reported in Lake Champlain but present in nearby waterbodies and pose a threat of invasion) were reported in 2026! posts.c: This is what we were up to while Outlook was down, if anyone was wondering. 🐟 Yesterday, @vtfishandwildlife fisheries biologists at the Ed Weed Fish Culture Station gave our team a demo on how they manage salmon traps in the fall! These salmon are captured during their fall migration up a small stream created by the hatchery's outflow. Biologists record data about the fish and take eggs from selected broodstock. Then, during the following spring and fall, young salmon raised at the hatchery are released into Lake Champlain and some inland waterways. This process is part of a broad effort to restore landlocked Atlantic salmon in Lake Champlain and support the lake's fishery. Photo 1: Sonya Vogel / LCBB; Photos 2-6: Emma Dannenberg/LCBP

posts.c: A bighorn sheep's face when someone says, "Nice antlers!" *bighorn sheep sigh* 😑 So, what's the difference between antlers and horns, anyway? Horns are a two-part structure. An interior portion of bone (which is an extension of the skull) is covered by an exterior sheath grown by specialized hair follicles (similar to human fingernails). Horns are usually found on both males and females of pronghorn, bison, and bighorn sheep. Antlers grow as an extension of the animal's skull. They are true bone, a single structure, and generally found only on males of the deer family. Antlers are also shed and re-grown each year, while horns are usually never shed and continue to grow throughout an animal's life. One exception to this rule is the pronghorn, which sheds and re-grows its horn sheath each year. Photo (NPS / Jacob W. Frank): 1. Bighorn sheep ram with large, curved horns. 2. Bull elk with large antlers. 3. Pronghorn buck with horns.

posts.c: This month, we recognize Suzan Shown Harjo, an enrolled Cheyenne citizen of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, whose lifelong advocacy has transformed the landscape of Indigenous rights, cultural preservation, and representation. A poet, writer, curator, and policy advocate, she has spent decades working to protect Native cultures, sacred places, and treaty rights while helping Indigenous communities reclaim and preserve their histories. As a founding trustee of the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Harjo played a vital role in creating a national space dedicated to sharing Native religious freedom and supporting the return of ancestral remains and cultural items to Tribal Nations. Her work has helped reshape how Indigenous peoples, cultures, and histories are represented in museums and public institutions across the country. posts.c: Last week we finished up our first adult Learn to Ride class! This free multi week collaboration between Old Spokes Home and Local Motion offered instruction for folks learning to ride for the first time, and for others needing a refresher. This class contributes to Old Spokes Home's overall mission of removing barriers to make bikes work for everyone. It also aligns perfectly with Local Motion's mission of making it safe, accessible, and fun for everyone to bike, walk, and roll in Vermont. The ability to ride a bike, and to ride it safely, opens up opportunities at any age! This class eases students into riding by focusing on balance first. Bikes without cranks and pedals act as adult striders, and as students became more comfortable they work up to bikes with pedals. posts.c: Saving a 136-year-old cast iron tub 🛁✨ Homeowners Harley and Ethan wanted to keep the original tub that came with the house, so @kevinoconnortoh and @dettmore101 took on the refinish together. Part 1: Stripping Suited up with respirators, since old paint can be lead-based Troweled on a ¼” layer of stripper paste Covered it with craft paper to keep it wet Let it work for 24 hours Bagged and sealed the paint, then scraped down to bare metal Part 2: Buffing + Painting Primed and sanded the outside Buffed the inside enamel with cerium oxide (a glass polish) and water Rinsed it, and the shine was back Flipped the tub and rolled on a matte black and white finish The matte finish hides the pitting and ties in with the tile Ready for another 130 years 🙌 📺 Watch today on @pbs (check local listings), and stream free Monday on @therokuchannel #TOHEssexCo #ThisOldHouse #TubRefinish #homeimprovement #beforeandafter

posts.c: Lava is hot. We thought you should know. We’ve been asked to elaborate. Fine. Lava is hot. It’s like making a grilled cheese, except the pan is a volcano on fire. Too much? Is it getting hot in here? Take two. Erupting lava at Hawaiʻi’s Kīlauea Volcano typically reaches around 2,100°F (1,150°C). That’s hot enough to turn rock into a glowing river of molten material. It’s also hot enough that getting too close can be extremely dangerous. Lava the view from a safe, designated viewing area, follow park guidance, and please resist the urge to find out just how hot it is firsthand. Some things are better left untouched. Lava is very high on that list. Has anyone touched lava lately? That’s not a question for you. We’re getting ahead of your questions. The answer, not that we know of. This is just a a friendly reminder to avoid any incidents. Plus even though lava is hot stuff, the pics are pretty cool to look at! NPS Photos: @hawaiivolcanoesnps /J. Wei

‘Get Yer Guy a Rock Tumbler’ Acrylic and oil on canvas 36 in x 18 in This painting has been a slow brew, started quickly, impulsively and gesturally as a revisit to a motif that I orbit: vignettes in the river. I’ve enjoyed the call and response dance we’ve been in step with, the many eras of ‘don’t overwork this,’ while also seeing that I still had something to search for. I enjoy that this painting was not given a job, but instead room for discovery. I am a sucker for the observational, figurative painting, though that part of my journey is not always legible in the final works. But this painting is more memory than anything else, a reference of many scenes and moments, finding what I love about the emblematic scene through that material, color search. I am grateful for the spiritual in painting- for lack of a better word - that routine calling into a void and the rare but special moment you catch a reply.

posts.c: A cosmic sampler 🍽️ These images are all Hubble observations of gravitational lenses, a phenomenon that occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object (such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies) bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. Hubble's targets show the diversity of how this effect can appear. Plus, these observations lay the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture many more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and ultraviolet prowess for individual objects. Learn more at the link in our bio! Image credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) Image description: A nine-image panel, each showing a different grav

posts.c: Rifle season opens this Saturday, and before everyone heads out into the woods, we wanted to help everyone have a safe and successful hunt by addressing a few Frequently Asked Questions we’ve been receiving: Q: Can I still hunt archery during rifle season? A: Rifle season & archery season are two completely separate seasons, each with their own regulations, with dates that overlap. Follow the regulations based on type of hunting you want to do, and which tags you have. For example, if a hunter wants to take a deer using their rifle tag, then they will hunt under rifle season regulations. If they’d like to take a deer using their archery tag, then they would hunt with their bow and under archery season regulations. Q: If a hunter is archery hunting, can they take an antlerless deer anywhere in the state? A: Yes, the archery season allows you to take an antlerless deer statewide. posts.c: Burying food scraps in your garden sounds like an easy way to feed your plants, but there’s a little more soil science involved than you might think. Organic matter doesn’t become plant food overnight. Soil microbes, fungi, and other decomposers have to break it down first, converting complex organic compounds into simpler nutrients that plant roots can eventually absorb. Here’s the catch: decomposition takes time, and fresh organic materials can temporarily tie up nutrients as microbes consume them to do their work. Depending on the material, its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and how quickly it breaks down, burying food scraps can actually delay nutrient availability rather than give plants an immediate boost. Materials like raw animal tissue also need time to decompose, which can make nutrient release unpredictable. The real lesson is that feeding your soil isn’t just about what you bury, but how quickly that material becomes available to your plants. Finished compost has already gone th

posts.c: We’re travelling with Doodle again, and again with @akasaair 🐶✈️ After our last flight, I got so many DMs asking how I prepare Doodle, crate train him, which crate we use and what I pack, so here’s everything I do before we fly. Honestly, most of the preparation happens before you even reach the airport. 🐾 Crate prep: I keep Doodle’s crate around for a few days before the flight so he can get comfortable going in, chilling and sleeping in it. 📦 Right-size crate: Doodle’s crate is 32 inches. Make sure your pet can comfortably stand, turn around and lie down. I also use a crate with removable wheels for easier handling. 🧸 Familiar comforts: His familiar comforter and favourite toy always go inside, something that smells like home helps him feel more settled. For anxious pets: If your pet gets anxious, speak to your vet about vet-approved calming support, which may be started a few days to a week before travel. posts.c: Chilly fall temperatures are blanketing the Champlain region, but below the surface of the lake, the waters will soon be stirring. Changing surface water temperatures trigger a natural process known as fall turnover. As fall arrives, surface waters lose heat to the air and become denser as they cool, allowing them to sink deeper into the lake. As autumn progresses, Lake Champlain’s layers become closer in temperature. This uniformity allows wind to more easily mix the water column, bringing deeper, nutrient-rich water upward while transporting oxygen-rich surface waters downward. Learn more about the phenomenon of lake turnover and what it means for aquatic ecosystems in Lake Champlain from our latest Nature Note - link in bio.🔗

posts.c: When Yellowstone was established in 1872, the National Park Service did not yet exist (and wouldn't until 1916). The park's first civilian superintendents lacked experience, funds, and a workforce to protect the park from exploitation. Eventually, Company M, First U.S. Cavalry of Ft. Custer, Montana Territory, answered the call to come to Yellowstone in 1886. This started the 30+ years of military protection of Yellowstone National Park. From the beginnings of Yellowstone to modern day, and all the time in between, we thank those who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces and continue to serve in a different uniform for the NPS. #VeteransDay 👉 Take a walking tour of the Fort Yellowstone Historic District or check out our virtual tour to learn more: https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/yell-tour-fort-yellowstone.htm (available in our bio) Photos (from the NPS Historical Archive and Jacob W. Frank): 1. Mounted cavalry drill on Fort Yellowstone's Parade Ground in Mammoth Hot Springs (c. 1910) 2.

posts.c: Between teaching painting, communications work, and the many moving parts of public art, studio has been a hard reach, but I’m always (over and over) finding my way back to my own studio practice. Sometimes the studio itself feels like a habit I have fallen out of; the space is so overwhelming when I return, I don’t know where to start. Recently, though, I’ve found drawing and little making sessions throughout the week make those precious studio sessions so much more vibrant, tactile, and generative. These days, the paintings have strayed from the “work plan,” the “proposal” or “elevator pitch.” That’s all relegated to keeping the public art, communications, and teaching curriculum to their strict but messy timelines. posts.c: Powering up research!☀️⚡ Last week, space station astronauts installed the eighth and final roll-out solar array (ROSA), completing a five-year power upgrade. Roll-out solar arrays have a lightweight and compact design that launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation. Despite being about half the size of the legacy arrays, the eight additional roll-out solar arrays boost the station’s power generation by more than 160 kilowatts. Together, the arrays provide increased power for daily operations and hundreds of research investigations that benefit humanity and support future exploration missions. Following prior testing on space station, the roll-out solar arrays have also been used on NASA’s Dart mission, showcasing space station’s essential role as a testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.
posts.hd: Final roll-out solar array installed on space station

posts.c: 🍟 80 YEARS OF FRENCH FRY HISTORY! Since 1946, Al’s French Frys in South Burlington, Vermont, has been serving up crispy golden fries and classic roadside favorites. What started as a small roadside fry stand founded by Al and Genevieve Rusterholz grew into one of Vermont’s most beloved food institutions. In 2010, Al’s earned the prestigious James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award, recognizing its place in American food culture. Nearly eight decades later, the tradition lives on with the same old-school charm that made this place special in the first place. Some things never go out of style, and a good order of French fries is definitely one of them! 📍 Al’s French Frys – South Burlington, VT

posts.c: A Statement from the City of Burlington The City of Burlington is committed to building and sustaining respectful, meaningful relationships with the Missisquoi Abenaki and the broader Indigenous communities with historical and contemporary ties to this region. I want to be clear that the City Council’s decision on May 18th not to accept the proposed statue to replace the former Chief Greylock statue was a municipal decision about public art; it was not intended to question or invalidate the identity or heritage of the Missisquoi Abenaki. posts.c: Asparagus is a perennial because it has an underground storage system that keeps it coming back year after year. The crown, a cluster of buds and roots just below the soil, stores carbohydrates that fuel new spear growth every spring. Its deep, established root system also helps the plant access water and nutrients beyond the reach of many shallow-rooted vegetables. Here’s the interesting part: those feathery ferns aren’t just extra foliage. They’re the plant’s solar panels. Through photosynthesis, they capture sunlight and convert it into sugars, which are transported down to the crown and stored as energy reserves. The more energy the crown accumulates during the growing season, the more resources it has to produce healthy spears in the seasons ahead. That’s why harvesting asparagus too early can set the plant back. Every spear you cut is a potential fern that could have been producing energy for the underground crown. Letting those spears mature allows the plant to build the reserve

posts.c: I came across these beautiful words recently and they kind of stayed with me. ‘If you love one, you usually love them all. Interior design, fashion, art, architecture. Obsessed with it allll. The way light transforms a space. The way fabric carries movement. How color sets a mood before words even arrive. A well-placed object. A clean line. A sudden curve. It is all storytelling through form, texture, silence, and shape. Beauty lives in details. And those who notice, feel it everywhere.’ I think that last line is what stayed with me the most.🫀 I have always enjoyed capturing life around me. Sharing some of my photos from the archives, which have made me realise I really should pick up my camera a little more often Hope you enjoy them. posts.c: Earth’s protective ozone layer is still on track for long-term recovery, despite a larger Antarctic ozone hole this year. The 2026 ozone hole is the 7th-largest ozone hole since NASA began tracking it in 1979. This year, the ozone hole reached its maximum extent of 10.5 million square miles on September 18. However, the ozone hole could have been 1 to 2 million square miles larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were two decades ago. posts.c: It's #NationalBisonDay, and we've got some bison facts! 1️⃣ Bison are the largest land mammal in North America Male bison (bulls) weigh up to 2,000 pounds and stand 6 feet tall, while females (cows) weigh up to 1,000 pounds and reach a height of 4-5 feet. Bison calves can weigh 30–70 pounds at birth. 2️⃣ Bison may be big, but they're also fast They are extremely agile and can run up to 30 miles per hour! 3️⃣ You can judge a bison's mood by its tail When it hangs down and swishes naturally, the bison is usually calm. If the tail is standing straight up, watch out! It may be ready to charge. No matter what a bison's tail is doing though, remember that they are unpredictable and can charge at any moment. Every year, there are regrettable accidents caused by people getting too close to these massive animals. It's great to love the bison but always be sure to love them from a distance of at least 25 yards (23 meters). 4️⃣ Bison love a good salad They primarily eat grasses, weeds and leafy p

posts.c: I think I found Burlington, Vermont’s best new hotel room. And wait until you see the views from the ninth floor. 😍🌅 Meet the Artist Studio at @theharborvale, overlooking Lake Champlain and downtown Burlington from one of the coolest private terraces in the city. This isn’t your typical hotel room. The 550-square-foot suite has a separate bedroom and living space, a kitchenette, a beautiful bathroom with a soaking tub and separate shower, and the real showstopper: a private outdoor terrace with rocking chairs, lounge seating and sweeping views of Lake Champlain and the Adirondacks. Coffee in the morning, cocktails at sunset. I could spend hours out here watching the boats on the lake. ⛵️ And if you haven’t heard of The Harborvale yet, it’s because this downtown Burlington hotel just underwent a complete $19 million transformation. Formerly the Courtyard by Marriott Burlington Harbor, the property has been reimagined from top to bottom and is now part of Marriott’s Autograph Collection,

posts.c: Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Hold on like a seahorse—there are plenty of them here and so much more to discover! Just swipe left and sea. African penguins are back in a newly expanded habitat! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. There’s so much to discover in Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar from flamboyant cuttlefish to garden eels. Swim over to the link in bio for

posts.c: Hubble (along with ground-based telescopes) revealed that the expansion rate of our universe is accelerating! Soon, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will study the “dark energy” behind this expansion with its large field of view and infrared vision. Its treasure trove of data will include tens of thousands of exploding stars and hundreds of millions of distant galaxies, tracing the universe’s expansion across nearly all of cosmic history! Hubble's key observations led to dark energy's discovery (even helping earn a Nobel prize in physics!) and the mission will work with Roman to continue investigating this enigma. As we gear up for its first images, we'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy. Check the link in our bio for more! #NASA #Hubble #Roman #astrophysics #space

posts.c: A bear-y cool week 🐻‍❄️🧊 San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance is proud to celebrate polar bears this week alongside @polarbearsinternational and other incredible partners, raising awareness of increasing human-wildlife conflict as melting sea ice drives more polar bears ashore. Across the Arctic, these coexistence efforts are helping people and polar bears safely share the landscape. Through the integration of science, wildlife care, strategic partnerships and a commitment to turning research into conservation action, the Alliance works to secure a future for this special species. This approach generates critical knowledge to inform management decisions and protect polar bears in their native habitat. 📸: @polarbearsinternational #polarbearweek #sandiegozoo

posts.c: You've likely heard of geysers and hot springs, but what about fumaroles? Fumaroles (or steam vents) are the hottest hydrothermal features in Yellowstone, with temperatures up to 280 F (138 C)! 🔥 Because they are so hot and contain very little water, the water boils away before reaching the surface. Then, steam and other gases emerge from the feature's vent, sometimes making hissing or whistling sounds. Roaring Mountain is a wonderful place to enjoy the sights and sounds of fumaroles, especially on cooler days! 👉 Learn more about fumaroles at: go.nps.gov/YELLhydrothermalfeatures (link in our "Learn More" highlight) Photo (NPS / Ashton Hooker): Roaring Mountain on a chilly winter day.
posts.hd: Fumaroles are Yellowstone's hottest steam vents

posts.c: Each autumn, we return to Twilight of the Idols, our seasonal porter brewed with coffee and cinnamon and conditioned on vanilla beans. Its origins precede Hill Farmstead, reaching back to Denmark in 2009. Shaun and Ryan Witter-Merithew first met in 2007. Two years later, as Shaun prepared to leave his brewing position at Nørrebro Bryghus and Fanø Bryghus, he enticed Ryan to move to Denmark to assume the role. They lived and brewed together for a month, beginning a friendship and collaboration that continues today. During that overlap, they established Grassroots Brewing to continue making beer together and maintain their connection to Denmark. Working on their first Christmas beer together (Fanø’s JulePorter), the idea for what would become Twilight of the Idols emerged from this period, taking its name from Friedrich Nietzsche’s text. posts.c: What if your fence could grow food instead of just taking up space? A fruit fence turns a simple vertical structure into a productive growing system, and passion fruit is perfect for the job because its climbing tendrils naturally grip onto nearby supports. The science is pretty cool. Passion fruit vines grow rapidly, spreading their leaves across a trellis to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. With enough light, water, and nutrients, the plant converts that energy into vigorous growth and eventually flowers and fruit. Training the vines vertically also helps you use space more efficiently, turning an otherwise unused area into productive growing space. And here’s the best part: a well-established passion fruit vine can produce an impressive harvest while giving you a living privacy screen. Instead of building a fence that only blocks the view, why not grow one that hides the eyesores, adds greenery, and produces delicious fruit? That’s a whole lot more value from the same footprint.
posts.hd: Passion fruit vines grown as a fruit fence

posts.c: Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. It might be small but it makes a strong statement 💚🌿 #plants #plantstyling #design #beforeandafter #babygirl Low planter from @fayraystudio

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how birds stay warm during winter? Chickadees grow feathers that can keep them up to 100 degrees F warmer than the surrounding air temperature. Waterfowl exhibit counter-current heat exchange in their limbs, which enables them to stand in cold water. Other adaptations include roosting with heads tucked into back feathers to conserve heat and staying active by retrieving food stored during the autumn months. 👉 Want to learn more? Visit the link in our “Learn More” highlight! Photos (NPS / Jim Peaco & Jacob W. Frank): (1) Mountain chickadee (2) Mallards on Alum Creek

posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt
posts.cp: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, (or whatever your favorite cheese is!), dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. Ours is a pretty old model, so it’s too big compared to the much smarter ones available these days. 🤌🏼 - - - #livingroom #bedroom #bluebedroom #cosybedroom #bedroomideas

posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

posts.c: New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

posts.c: If there’s one thing I’m going to do while traveling, it’s find a local flea market! 🇩🇰 While in Copenhagen, I spent a rainy Saturday morning wandering through Frederiksberg Flea Market, and it was well worth the visit. Think vintage Danish ceramics, artwork, antique furniture, and plenty of odds and ends that require a little digging (my favorite kind of shopping). This market has a real neighborhood yard sale feel, and the prices were pretty reasonable, too! 📍 Frederiksberg Flea Market (Frederiksberg Loppetorv) John Winthers Plads, behind Frederiksberg City Hall, Copenhagen 🗓️ When: Saturdays, April–October ⏰ Hours: 9 AM–3 PM 💰 Good to know: Free entry and cash only, so make sure to bring Danish kroner! Definitely one to add to your Copenhagen itinerary if you love vintage shopping as much as I do! #copenhagen #thrifting #thriftedhomedecor

posts.c: Best of my time in west mt airy 🩷 the most magical cottagey rowhouse on the most charming street- I put a lot of love into this place to make it feel like home for me- painted the whole dang thing, replaced the light fixtures, planted a whole bunch of plants, and more! I enjoyed her for 2.5 years but it was time for change! I went through a big breakup here- my first and only relationship that lasted 8 years. I lived here alone for a year and a half, becoming a single cat mommy of two, while I healed and found my way back to myself, found new hobbies (tennis, rock climbing, knitting, golfing, following baseball again), prioritizing my friendships and making new ones, learning how to spend comfortable time alone and figure things out for myself after living with someone for so long. I imagine I’ll find my way back to mt airy since I love her so much, but for now I’m back in the city and excited to decorate my new solo (!!!) apt and for all that comes next 💖

Optical illusions happen because your eyes send information to your brain, and your brain immediately starts making educated guesses about what it is seeing. Usually that works perfectly, but certain patterns, colors, shadows, and shapes can trick those shortcuts, making still images appear to move or identical lines look completely different. The best part is that even after someone explains the illusion, your brain may still refuse to cooperate. You can literally know two squares are the same color and your brain will look you dead in the eye and say, “No, they absolutely are not.” Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

As we continue to grieve Nipho alongside you, we’re sharing what we’ve learned about his passing, along with an update on his half-brother, Sundzu. Inhlonipho “Nipho," passed away on Wednesday after a brief battle with one of the most serious diseases facing the world’s elephants, known as EEHV-HD (elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus hemorrhagic disease). EEHV-HD, which poses no risk to people or other wildlife, is caused by a naturally occurring virus found in Asian and African elephants around the world, both in their native habitats and human care. Most elephants will contract the virus in their lifetime, and many carry it without becoming ill. Younger elephants are particularly vulnerable to complications. Nipho’s illness came on and progressed unusually fast. Our team began treatment right away, even before a definitive diagnosis, and we are continuing to look closely at his case to understand what happened. It is with exceptionally heavy hearts that we share the passing of Inhlonipho “Nipho,” an incomparable African savanna elephant at the San Diego Zoo. As with all wildlife at the Zoo, Nipho’s wellness was monitored closely each day. When his team noticed signs of stomach discomfort and lethargy, the Zoo’s wildlife health experts provided prompt, around-the-clock care. Despite their tireless efforts, Nipho passed away today with his wildlife care specialists by his side. Nipho was deeply rooted in the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance family. He was born at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to his mom, Umngani, who continues to thrive in the Elephant Valley herd. Throughout his life at both the Safari Park and the Zoo, he opened the door for countless guests to connect with his endangered species, a fitting legacy for an elephant whose name means “courteous.” As he grew older, Nipho followed the path of young males in native habitats, who leave their family herds and may form bachelor herds to

held.c: 2 weeks since Kiki’s accident / hip dysplasia diagnosis ❤️ And 2 weeks without walkies for Kiki 🥺 we might do our first short 5 minute walk today, for a change of scenery. Kiki is definitely making sure we’re aware of the fact that she is EXTREMELY BORED. But the more bed rest she gets, the faster we hope she’ll go back to normal! She is now walking normally without limping, but is still lifting her paw when she’s standing still. Very very eager to jump around, but we do find that she’s taking more time to go up the stairs (when we catch her doing it)… instead of zooming upstairs like a breeze, she goes step by step… 🥹 Which is also making us realise that even though they’re still puppies on the inside, they’re getting older on the outside. In fact, it’s Kiki’s 7th birthday in two days! She also has her first hydrotherapy appointment tomorrow ❤️ #dog #beagle

held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. Ok people, It is Election Day and I hope you all know what that means! Time to go VOTE!! If you are like me, you may be saddened by the current political state in our country. Party allegiance aside, so much of what is being talked about seems to be fueled by hatred, violence and struggle. While It can all feel overwhelming, I always try and remember that the actual people who live in this country are loving, kind, hard working and resilient. When I was greeted with the above spread I was reminded about how great the people are and how important It is to elect leaders who think and act like us. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. Shoutout to whoever dialed in these cider doughnuts,
